datasheet.title: Casa Systems C100G Converged Cable Access Platform data sheet

devices.description: Casa C100G CMTS/CCAP - 13RU, 14 paired front/rear slots. Front and rear slot N are two halves of one logical position: a DOCSIS line card in front N requires its I/O partner in rear N.

gaps.note: The BDM2/BDM2m datasheet states "Total Power 300 W" in a technical specifications table headed "BDM2/2 m with 6+12 IO Card", whose RF connector row describes that card's six downstream and twelve upstream ports. The figure is the assembly's. A BDM position is TWO modules here - casa/bdm in a front bay and casa/io-6p12 in the paired rear bay, which is why casa/bdm already carries `pairs-with` - and no document we hold divides the 300 W between them. Writing it onto the front module would make the chassis total come out right and the answer to "what does a BDM front module draw" come out wrong, so neither half carries a figure and the chassis total stays a floor. The arithmetic does not settle it either way: 12 x 300 W lands on the C100G's stated 3.6 kW whether the 300 W is the pair or the front half with small rear cards. The C100G HIG corroborates the assembly reading and hedges it: Tables A-10 and A-11 both read "Approximately 300W per BDM" under titles scoping them to the BDM WITH its 6+12 I/O. THE LIBRARY IS CURRENTLY INCONSISTENT ABOUT THIS, ON PURPOSE AND VISIBLY. The three BDM variants carry NO power figure, for the reason above. The DQM and DCU cards added later DO carry one - DS8x8 220, DS8x96 320, DS8x192 350, US16x8 220, US16x4 150 - each with a `power-scope` provenance entry saying in the vendor's own words that the number covers the card WITH its I/O module and must not have a rear figure added to it. Both are defensible readings of the same problem: one keeps the per-module answer honest and the chassis total a floor, the other keeps the vendor's only published number reachable. They should not stay different once a pairing-scoped mechanism exists, and this is the record of which way each went and why, so that whoever unifies them is not guessing. THE THREE REAR RF I/O CARDS ADDED LATER FALL ON THE SAME SIDE OF THIS AS THE 6+12. casa/rfd, casa/rfu-16x8 and casa/ups-32x4 carry NO power figure, because Tables A-8 and A-9 give their port counts and connector types and no watts at all, and every figure Casa does publish for the slot is already the pair's - Table A-3 heads the DQM column "Maximum consumption with I/O module" and Table A-4 gives "Single DCU w/ RFU I/O" 200 W against "Single DCU w/ RFU UPS 32x4 I/O" 220 W for the same US16x8. Subtracting one from the other to get a rear card's share would be our arithmetic and would also be the wrong subtraction - the 20 W is the difference between two PAIRINGS, not between two I/O cards.
gaps.wanted: a pairable unit that can carry properties, so that a figure measured on a pair can be attached to the pair. The scope is now DATA - every card here declares `power-draw-scope: module-with-paired-io`, so a chassis sum knows not to add the rear partner and L30 catches it if one gains its own figure - but the scope says only THAT the figure covers a pair, not WHICH pair. The C100G HIG gives the same US16x8 200 W with the RFU I/O and 220 W with the RFU UPS 32x4, and the manifest can carry only one of them. Asking for "a per-module figure" was the wrong question: Casa states none, and one may not exist to be divided out. What is missing is the mechanism, and enough vendors doing this to design one from - Casa is the only one in the corpus.

gaps.note: The HIG body text states "Each fan assembly module has a maximum power consumption of 100W, totaling 300W across the three fan assemblies". Table A-2 of the same guide gives the row "Fan assembly (3)" as "330W maximum, 220W typical". Both are about the set of three and 300 is not 330. The contract takes 100 W because it is the only figure stated PER MODULE, which is the granularity a bay occupant needs; dividing 330 by three would be our arithmetic, not the vendor's. A chassis total is therefore 30 W light against the guide's own set figure, and no per-module typical exists at all.
gaps.wanted: a measurement from a running chassis, a vendor erratum, or a later revision of the guide that drops one of the two figures

gaps.note: Casa rates a power ENTRY module in amps and volts, never in watts. Table A-1 gives "Voltage -42 to -60VDC" and "Current 20A nominal per feed", and the chassis nameplate at Figure 1-3 gives "-48VDC, 30A per Feed (4+4 Feeds)" - but no document states a wattage, and deriving one means choosing a point the vendor left open: two current figures across a voltage range put V x I anywhere from about 810 W to 1800 W per feed. A power entry module also does not convert or regulate; it filters and distributes what the plant feeds it, so its rating is a current-carrying limit rather than the continuous output power-output-w means. The stated volts and amps are recorded in the contract's attrs; the L27 warning stays standing as the record that the watt figure is missing.
gaps.wanted: a wattage for the C100G power entry module from Casa - a nameplate photograph of the module itself would do it, or any document that rates it in watts rather than amps

a `power-draw-max-w` on each module this chassis accepts, from the vendor's own per-card table - Cisco publishes one per ambient, most vendors publish none, and until they land a module total is a floor

an `attrs.performance` section; `cpu`, `memory` in a missing `attrs.platform` section; one of `operating-temp`, `operating-temp-f2b`, `operating-temp-b2f` in a missing `attrs.environmental` section (profile `networking` - see spec/schemas/profiles.yaml) - unlocks the About panel, and comparison against other devices
`physical-context` on 33 bays (front 14, rear 19) - unlocks ENTITY-MIB / Redfish correlation and monitoring overlays

datasheet.title: Casa Systems C40G Converged Cable Access Platform data sheet

devices.description: Casa C40G CMTS/CCAP - 6RU, 6 paired front/rear slots. Takes the same line cards as the C100G but HORIZONTALLY, so the card is one model placed at rotate 90.

gaps.note: THE ORDERING SHEET SELLS FOUR CHASSIS AND THIS LIBRARY MODELS TWO. C40G_DS_RevA lists C40G-CHASSIS-AC and C40G-CHASSIS-DC, which are here, and C40G-CHASSIS-ACR and C40G-CHASSIS-DCR, described as "with Redundant Power and Cooling", which are not. The sheet gives the phrase and nothing else - no count, no which modules, no dimensions - and the installation guide never uses the word for a chassis variant. What the guide DOES say is that the C40G takes up to four 1100 W PSUs operating concurrently and that fewer than two cannot power a C40G-20, which tells you the supplies are redundant by population rather than by chassis. That makes the R variants most likely a populated bundle rather than different metal - but "most likely" is not a source, and inventing two configurations from a four-word description would put a guess where a part number goes.
gaps.wanted: a Casa or CommScope ordering guide saying what the R bundles contain - how many PSUs and fan modules, and whether the chassis itself differs at all

gaps.note: Casa says two things about this terminal and they do not agree. The prose in "Connecting the chassis to ground" says it "provides two M6 screws to connect a double-lug ground terminal cable". Figures 1-2 and 1-4 both DRAW three studs, in a 2x2 grid with the protective-earth mark in the fourth corner, and the two figures agree with each other. THE DRAWING IS FOLLOWED, and the model carries three. The figure is the only source that says anything about arrangement at all, so following the prose would mean inventing a layout for the two it describes; and a third stud has easy explanations - a spare, an alternate lug pitch - while a stud drawn twice that is not there has none. That is a judgement, not a reading, which is why it is filed here. THE PITCH IS NOT MEASURED FROM EITHER. It is borrowed from casa/ground-bolts@1, 15.3, off the maintainer`s hand-built C100G rear SVG. Figure 1-4 gives 13.2 across and 14.7 down for what must be one square grid - an 11 percent disagreement with itself, which is that figure`s anisotropy rather than a rectangular pattern.
gaps.wanted: a photograph of the C40G rear lower-left corner, which would settle the count and the pitch together in one look

gaps.note: The card band runs 37.5 to 386.7 in a body 432.95 wide, so it sits 37.5 from the left edge and 46.25 from the right - 8.75 mm out of centre, or 4.375 on the band's own centreline. Everything inside the band agrees with everything else; the question is whether the band is really off-centre in the metal, and nothing we hold answers it. IT IS NOT COSMETIC, and the AC input panel is where it bites. Its four C14 inlets sit behind the four front power supplies. Reflect the supply centres about the PANEL and the inlets are 1.2 out; reflect them about the CHASSIS - which is what walking round a box actually does - and they are 9.95 out. The gap between those two answers IS this asymmetry, and no arrangement of the parts inside the band can close it, because the disagreement is between the band and the chassis rather than within either. THE SUPPORTING NUMBERS ARE ALSO ODD IN THE SAME DIRECTION. The two front fan strips measure 36.0 wide each - equal, as you would expect - but leave 1.5 outside them on the left and 10.25 on the right. Two equal strips with unequal surrounds is exactly the shape of a band that has been positioned from one edge. NOT RESOLVED BY GUESSING, deliberately. Re-centring the band would move the two fan strips, the card bays on both faces, the PSU row, the PSU cover and the AC panel - and it would be one estimate reconciled against another, which this device's `pem-band-top-edge` note already records going wrong twice in opposite directions.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned C40G front or rear elevation from Casa, or a tape measure across a real chassis from its left edge to the first card slot and from the last card slot to its right edge

gaps.note: The PEM band's BOTTOM edge at 264.5 is agreed by every source and is not in doubt. Its TOP edge is known only to about 2 mm, and the three candidates each have support: 194.0 is the direct reading of Figure 1-4 and is impossible, because the card slot above ends at 194.82; 194.82 is flush against that slot; 196.0 is what the bays carry and is what the manifest now uses, on the argument that 194.82 is an accumulation of six DERIVED slot pitches (426.6 mm over 14 slots on the C100G, carried across) and that the front face shows a measured 1.48 mm margin in the equivalent position. That argument is sound but it is an argument, not a measurement, and the whole disagreement is six pixels at 2.982 px/mm. A tape measure on a real C40G, or any Casa drawing that dimensions the rear panel, would settle it in one number. FIGURE 1-12 HAS NOW BEEN LOOKED AT AND DOES NOT SETTLE IT, recorded so nobody spends the search twice. "C40G power entry module" is the only isolated drawing of this part and the first independent look anything has had at it. Its body measures 866 x 381 px for an aspect of 2.273. The modelled 158.0 x 68.5 is 2.307 and the superseded 158.0 x 70.5 is 2.241, and 2.273 lands 0.04 percent off the midpoint of those two - at 158.0 wide it implies a height of 69.51. IT IS EQUIDISTANT AND CONFIRMS NEITHER. This guide's isolated part drawings are in any case demonstrably about 10 percent wrong about their own aspect - Figure 1-20 draws a card at 12.54 whose real aspect is 11.34 - so a 1.5 percent lean is well inside the drawing's own error. THE NUMBER IS THEREFORE NOT MOVED. It has been moved twice already, in both directions, and a third move on evidence that splits the difference would be the reconciliation loop rather than an escape from it. What Figure 1-12 does confirm is the ARRANGEMENT, which is what a figure is good for: a bolted terminal cover across the top with three fasteners, a minus pair of studs above a plus pair inside two outlined blocks, two release levers standing proud of the body top and bottom, and the yellow disconnect-power label to their right - all of which casa/c40g-pem draws. RECORDED BECAUSE THE MODULE AND THE BAY NOW AGREE, which means nothing will ever flag this again - the fit check that found the original 2 mm discrepancy is satisfied by both being wrong together as easily as by both being right.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned C40G rear elevation, or a tape measure on the PEM opening

datasheet.title: Celestica DS1000 1U 48-port 1GbE Data Center Switch datasheet (cls_branded_datasheet_DS1000_090924)

devices.description: Celestica DS1000 - an OCP-accepted 1U management and top-of-rack switch with 48 x 10/100/1000BASE-T RJ45 ports in three ganged blocks of sixteen and 8 x 10G SFP+ in one 2 x 4 stacked cage, all on a black front bezel with the four system lamps, the RJ45 management and console jacks and two USB 2.0 ports between the second and third blocks. Two 550 W hot-swap CRPS supplies sit at the right of the rear and three fixed 40 mm fans behind round grilles at the left. Ports number 1-48 down each column, odd on the top row; the SFP+ cage numbers 49-56 the same way. Front-to-back and back-to-front builds.

gaps.wanted: A drawing of the lid, underside and side walls. The Foleon three-quarter renders show the lid carries two pressed finger recesses and a rectangular label panel, and the right wall a row of rail screws and a vent - visible, not measurable at an angle. The guide draws only the front and rear. These four faces are sized and left bare rather than guessed.
Which operating range is right. Datasheet: 0 C to 45 C at 900 m, 5 % to 90 % humidity. Guide spec table: 5 - 40 C (both airflows), 40 - 60 % operating humidity. attrs carries the datasheet's figures.

An orthographic view of the rear printing. The three-quarter render prints, beside each fan and supply, a numeral with a fan or power glyph and a triangle, turned on end; the guide's grey CAD prints none of it. Only the numerals are drawn, at positions proportional from the render.

The DS1000 guide has no LED section - no table for the four system lamps, the RJ45 jack lamps or the SFP+ light pipes. The status lamps carry the names printed under them and nothing else is claimed. The DS2000 guide's tables for the same lamp names are a sibling's, not this device's.

Orderable part numbers for the 2000 W supply and the fan module. The datasheet's ordering table lists only the system (R4028-F9002-A1) and the guide's FRU pages give removal steps without part numbers, so both components are named for their form rather than their PN.

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9000 Series ASR 9001 Router - a 2 RU fixed-port aggregation services router with an integrated route processor, four fixed 10 GE SFP+ ports, two modular port adapter bays and 120 Gbps of fabric. Everything is on the front face: both MPA bays, both power supplies, the side-mounted fan tray and every port. The rear is a plain louvred panel.

gaps.note: HALF OF THIS IS FIXED. The ASR 9001-S's two licence-disabled SFP+ ports and its disabled modular bay are now stated: roc-ops/Portrayal#193 widened `component-attrs` to accept a placement id as well as a component name, and `bay-attrs` already took a bay path, so sfp-plus-2, sfp-plus-3 and mpa-1 carry `enabled: no` and the licence that unlocks them, in that configuration alone. WHAT IS STILL NOT SAYABLE is the 60 Gbps figure: a configuration can now say what is true of a PART and still cannot override an attr of the DEVICE, so this chassis carries the 120 Gbps switching capacity for both models and the -S's half-capacity lives in prose.
gaps.wanted: a way for a configuration to override a device-level attr - the same widening one level up. docs/what-a-configuration-cannot-say.md now records which two thirds of that shape are closed and why this one is not.

gaps.note: Table 4 of the fixed-port install guide gives the 10MHz and 1PPS connectors as DIN 1.0/2.3. The standards registry has no key for it - sma, smb, mcx and f-type are there, DIN 1.0/2.3 is not - so these two openings are declared as panel cutouts at their measured size rather than composed from a std/ part. Substituting sma or smb would name a connector Cisco does not. THE REASON WAS vendor-silent AND THAT WAS THE WRONG TOKEN. Cisco is not silent - it names the connector outright. What is missing is a panel-cutout dimension, which is needs-drawing, and the difference matters because the two tokens ask different things of a reader: vendor-silent reads as closed until better documents appear, needs-drawing reads as an errand somebody can run today. The correction came from asr9k-cards, who had just been wrong in exactly this direction about the XFP - concluding a figure was unsourceable after searching the intake rather than the standards - and found it in INF-8077i ten minutes after looking somewhere else. IEC 61169-8 is the somewhere else here, and nobody has opened it yet.
gaps.wanted: a std/din-1-0-2-3 part and its standards.yaml key. THE CONNECTOR IS STANDARDISED, so a sourced dimension exists to be found rather than estimated - DIN 1.0/2.3 is specified in IEC 61169-8, and any manufacturer's bulkhead-jack panel drawing carries the D-hole figure. std/mcx is the worked example of exactly this being done properly earlier tonight: registered from IEC 61169-36 / CECC 22220 at 4.95 x 4.50 with confidence verified, replacing an estimate that was 28 percent too small. This should be done the same way, and until it is, an sma or smb standing in would be a plausible wrong answer - which is the failure mode this project keeps having to dig back out

gaps.note: cisco/a9k-pwr-3kw-ac@1 states 142.78 mm wide. Three of them need 428.34 mm and this chassis's power shelf interior measures 416.50, so they do not fit - lint L13 flagged the overlap directly when they were placed at the measured centres. Against that, the stencil's shape box for the 'A9K Power Module' master reads 0.5477 in, which is 139.12 mm at the stencil's 1:10 scale, and my own measurement of the three openings in the ASR 9006 front master gives 138.35, 137.50 and 138.23. Those two agree to under a millimetre, and three at 139.12 come to 417.36 against a 416.50 shelf - the arithmetic a shelf that holds exactly three ought to produce. The 142.78 is most likely the art measured over something that is not the module's seating width, the same class of error as reading a card's shape box instead of its art. The bays here are sized to the measured openings, so the chassis is right and the component and the chassis disagree by about 3.7 mm until someone re-measures the master.

gaps.note: STILL OPEN; the numbers around it changed. This file and the ASR 9010 manifest carry pitches that differ - 46.605 here against 44.332 there - for two chassis that take the same cards. For a while the 9010 was divided unevenly to fit a 1.81 in (46.0 mm) RSP-880; under the card standard every card is drawn 41.4 thick, so that reason is gone and the 9010 is again divided evenly across its measured cage. The two pitches still differ because the two measured cages differ, which is not a contradiction. HERE THE EVEN SIX-WAY DIVISION OF THE 279.63 mm CAGE IS STILL AN ASSUMPTION: at 41.4 per card any division giving each slot at least 41.4 admits every card, so the card size cannot discriminate between an even split and an uneven one. The even division is kept because it is what the cage measures and nothing here favours another. Neither this master nor the 9010 master prints slot labels or draws cage dividers, which is why both were assumptions in the first place - the 9904, 9906, 9910, 9912 and 9922 all have a ruler in the picture and these two do not.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned front elevation of the ASR 9006, or a per-slot width from any Cisco document

gaps.note: Two figures in b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf give the ASR 9006 body width differently. Table 13 "Cisco ASR 9000 Series Routers Physical Descriptions" (p130) says 17.50 inches (44.45 cm). Figure 9 "Cisco ASR 9006 Router Chassis Footprint Dimensions - Top Down View" (p24) dimensions the same body at 17.38 inches (44.15 cm). Same measure, same part, 3 mm apart, so this is a real conflict and not two scopes. The manifest carries 44.45 because the spec table is authoritative for overall dimensions and because Cisco's own Visio master independently records 1.9 in at 1:10 over the flanges, which back-solves to Table 13's split once the 19.05 mm flange protrusion is subtracted. The likeliest reconciliation is that 17.50 is over the outer skin and 17.38 is the sheet metal at the section plane Figure 9 cuts, but no document we hold says that, so it is not written as though one does. The height is unaffected - both sources and the stencil agree on 17.50 in there.
gaps.wanted: a Cisco mechanical drawing with a tolerance, or a tape measure on a real ASR 9006

gaps.note: The power modules load from the front but their inlets are on the rear, and the only artwork we hold for that rear panel is the stencil's ASR-9006-AC Rear master, which draws the VERSION 1 tray: three IEC inlets labelled M2, M1, M0 left to right (mirrored from the front's M0, M1, M2) with the legend "100-240V 50/60 Hz 16A MAX (3X)" and a yellow warning label. This chassis is modelled as version 2, which has four modules and therefore four inlets, and no figure in any document we hold shows the version 2 rear panel. Rather than mirror three inlets into four and invent a pitch, the rear carries the inlet panel's outer band only. The DC rear is a further unknown again - there is no ASR-9006-DC master in the stencil at all.
gaps.wanted: a figure or photograph of the version 2 AC rear panel, and of the DC rear panel

gaps.note: The air filter is real, sourced and correctly typed as a bay - Table 17 of b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf places it along the right side accessible from the rear, and Figure 207 shows the panel and its thumb screw. What is NOT sourced is its geometry. Figure 207 is a three-quarter perspective view with no dimension lines on it, so its aspect is foreshortened and it fails gate 1 as a source of absolute size. The filter's 52 mm width and its 8 mm standoff from the rear edge are read as fractions of that figure and anchored to the chassis depth, and its height is set to the card cage band rather than measured. Treat the filter's extent as the one feature here that a tape measure would most likely move. Its presence, its side, its access direction and the fact that it is user-replaceable are all stated in words by the guide and are not in doubt.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned side elevation of the ASR 9006, or the air filter's own spare-part drawing

gaps.note: ONE OPENING IS LEFT, AND THIS NOTE USED TO SAY SEVEN. FT0 and FT1 are bays now - they accept cisco/asr-9006-fan@1, whose own envelope is the measurement of these very openings - and M0 to M3 became the pm-0 to pm-2 power bays some time before that, which this note had not caught up with. What is still a cutout with no occupant is the right-side air filter, 52 x 279.63. THE ORIGINAL POINT STANDS FOR THAT ONE: a cutout with no part is invisible to every rule - a missing ref lints, an absent bay does not - so a reader could reasonably think this chassis has no filter. It has one; it is waiting.
gaps.wanted: the ASR 9006 chassis air filter, which is the last of the seven openings this gap was opened for

gaps.note: RENAMED FROM blank-faces AND REWORDED, because both faces stopped being blank and the gap was still describing the file as it stood two commits ago. NO DOCUMENT WE HOLD SHOWS EITHER FACE OF AN ASR 9006 - that part is unchanged and is the gap. What each face now carries is derived from a figure of a DIFFERENT face, which is a weaker thing than being drawn and is why the gap stays open. The bottom carries the rack mounting surface, because the plane is dimensioned in Figure 9's top-down view and necessarily cuts the underside at the same depth it cuts the top. The left carries one of the three NEBS bonding points, because Figure 58 callouts a left-side pad and its position is INFERRED from a three-quarter view rather than dimensioned. Neither is a bottom or left drawing; both are a fact about the chassis that has to intersect this face. Everything else about these two faces - feet, labels, vents, plates, the flange profile - is still unknown, and the guide's "There is no clearance requirement for the left side of the chassis" (b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf p1172) is consistent with a solid unfeatured panel without proving one. The sizes are from Table 13 and Figure 9 and are right, so the rack elevation and the 3D box are right, which is the load these two views actually carry.
gaps.wanted: a six-face photograph set, or the mechanical drawings behind Figure 9

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9010 Router - the 21RU, ten-slot member of the ASR 9000 Series Aggregation Services Routers. Cards mount VERTICALLY across the full width of the cage: the two CENTRE slots, 4 and 5, are reserved for a redundant RSP pair, with four line card slots either side of them. A cable management tray runs along the top, two stacked fan trays and a front air intake sit below the cage, and two power shelves fill the bottom. Modelled as a BARE CAGE: every slot is a bay a card component drops into, not a traced faceplate.

gaps.note: THE CARD BAY EXTENTS ARE A FAMILY STANDARD, NOT MEASUREMENTS OF THIS CAGE. All ten slots are 41.4 x 395.7 with a 41.4 x 355.6 opening, chosen so one card component fits every ASR 9000 chassis. Two of the three numbers are Cisco figures: 395.7 is the fourth-generation "includes ejector bracket/lever" envelope, which a lab measurement of a real A9K-RSP880 supports at about 15 1/2 in (roc-ops/Portrayal#16), and 355.6 is the Table A-10 plate length, which the cage measured off the stencil (354.95) matches to 0.65 mm. The 41.4 thickness is the figure Cisco states most often and has NOT been measured; the 43.7 of the original-generation cards and the 46.0 of the RSP-880 are overridden by it as a modelling decision. The slot division is the measured cage split ten ways, which is arithmetic: the stencil master draws the cage as one undivided rectangle, and no per-slot width was found in the Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide, the Hardware Installation Guide or the Overview and Reference Guide. The danger this entry exists to record still applies: a fit check compares a bay to a component and neither to the world, so a standard shared by both passes it whether or not it is true.
gaps.wanted: a caliper reading of an ASR 9000 card thickness (requested on roc-ops/Portrayal#16), a dimensioned front elevation or per-slot width for the ASR 9010, or a tape measure on a real one

gaps.note: cisco/a9k-pwr-3kw-ac@1 states 142.78 mm wide. Three of them need 428.34 mm and this chassis's power shelf interior measures 416.50, so they do not fit - lint L13 flagged the overlap directly when they were placed at the measured centres. Against that, the stencil's shape box for the 'A9K Power Module' master reads 0.5477 in, which is 139.12 mm at the stencil's 1:10 scale, and my own measurement of the three openings in the ASR 9006 front master gives 138.35, 137.50 and 138.23. Those two agree to under a millimetre, and three at 139.12 come to 417.36 against a 416.50 shelf - the arithmetic a shelf that holds exactly three ought to produce. The 142.78 is most likely the art measured over something that is not the module's seating width, the same class of error as reading a card's shape box instead of its art. The bays here are sized to the measured openings, so the chassis is right and the component and the chassis disagree by about 3.7 mm until someone re-measures the master.
gaps.wanted: a re-measurement of the 'A9K Power Module' stencil master, or a Cisco dimension for the version 1 power module

gaps.note: The ASR 9010's two fan trays occupy the band between the card guide bar at 566.51 mm and the front air intake grille at 673.60 mm - 107.09 mm for the pair, which is measured and solid. Where one ended and the other began was NOT measured. Scanning that band finds a dark separator at about 605.8 mm, but it does not bisect the band (39.3 mm above it, 66.9 mm below), so it was read as internal faceplate detail rather than the boundary, and an EVEN split was recorded as the right inference: the master labels both trays "ASR-9010-FAN", so they are the same part stacked twice and the same part is the same height. RESOLVED, AND THE SEPARATOR WAS THE BOUNDARY AFTER ALL. Dismissing it assumed the two trays fill the band, and they do not - two trays of 33.32 come to 66.64 of 107.09. cisco/asr-9010-fan was measured off this chassis's own front master at y 571.44 to 604.76, and that bottom edge and the separator at 605.8 agree to 1.04 mm: two measurements taken for different reasons, landing on the same line. Both trays are seated there now rather than split evenly, so the placement is measured and the inference is retired. What the band holds BELOW them - about 34 mm between the second tray and the grille starting at 675.08 - is still unnamed, and the band stays ONE cutout because a single opening with two trays in the top of it and intake beneath is what the guide's own cooling-path figure (Figure 71) draws.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned front elevation, or the ASR-9010-FAN spare-part drawing

gaps.note: The card slots are bays and accept the line card and RSP blank. THE FAN TRAYS HAVE SINCE LEFT THIS LIST - cisco/asr-9010-fan now exists and both are seated as bays at the positions its own size provenance measured off this chassis's front master. The eight power module positions and the air filter are still NOT modelled as bays, because a bay must name a component that fits it and library/components/cisco/ carries no version 2 or 3 power module and no filter. Their openings ARE measured and are drawn as cutouts, so the metal is right and only the occupants are missing. The power shelf openings are 13.96 to 431.66 mm at y 811.74 and 873.33; the fan band is 566.51 to 673.60. Pointing them at the line card blank would lint clean and claim something false - a 41.4 x 395.7 filler plate does not cover a power module opening.
gaps.wanted: an ASR 9010 fan tray, the version 2 and 3 AC and DC power modules, and the chassis air filter

gaps.note: The cisco logo, the "ASR 9000 Series" wordmark and an "OPEN" legend are printed on the CABLE MANAGEMENT TRAY, not on chassis metal - the stencil master draws them inside that band. Per the skill, text on a part's own face is that part's silkscreen, so this chassis deliberately carries none and the tray is not modelled as a placement for want of a component. The band itself is measured (0 to 163.76 mm) and drawn as decor, so the metal is right and only the printing and the tray are absent. This is the same decision taken on the ASR 9006's fan tray door.
gaps.wanted: a cable management tray component carrying its own branding

gaps.note: THE BOTTOM IS THE ONLY FACE OF THIS CHASSIS WITH NO SOURCE, and it is not a gap in this file's research. There is no bottom view of ANY ASR 9000 chassis anywhere in the 78-document intake: every figure caption in all 65 PDFs was searched for "Bottom View", "underside" and "bottom of the chassis", and the result is zero hits. That is a fact about how Cisco documents a rack chassis rather than about this model - a face that sits on rack rails and is never serviced gets no figure. The face is SIZED correctly from Table 13, so a rack elevation and the 3D box are the right shape; what it lacks is any statement of what is on it. Nothing is invented to fill it, and no region is added naming the absence, because a check passed by annotating that you have nothing is worse than a check failed honestly. THIS HOLDS THE CHASSIS AT CAPABILITY 2. Front, rear, top, left and right all now carry sourced content; the bottom alone does not, and level 3's implementation requires content on all six. The written design asks only that six faces be "present, sized, and mutually consistent", which this file satisfies - the content requirement comes from `_has_content`, which was written for level 1. See docs/deliberately-empty-faces.md.
gaps.wanted: a bottom elevation, a photograph of the underside, or a way for a view to declare itself deliberately empty so that empty-by-verification counts where empty-by-omission does not

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9000 Series ASR 9901 Router - a 2 RU fixed-port provider-edge router with an integrated route processor and 456 Gbps of fabric. Everything a user touches is on the front: forty-two ports across the top in five blocks - eight 1GE, twelve dual-rate 10/1GE, two 100GE, twelve more 10/1GE and eight more 1GE - and below them the timing, management and console jacks, nine alarm lamps, a four-character LED matrix display and the shelf power switch. The rear carries three fan trays and two 1.6 kW supplies. Airflow is front to back, and nothing seats on the front face at all.

gaps.note: The fixed-port install guide names the Connectivity Management Processor port only in the front-panel callouts, and Table 4 has no row for it; the series overview guide describes CMP as a secondary processor with its own front-panel management Ethernet port, with no rate. The 9901 data sheet lists it without one.
gaps.wanted: the CMP jack rate, so the port can state a `speed`.

gaps.note: TWO CISCO DOCUMENTS GIVE THIS CHASSIS TWO HEIGHTS. The ASR 9901 Router Data Sheet (c78-740540) Table 2 says "Height: 3.43 inches (8.7 cm)", which is 87.12 mm. The fixed-port Hardware Installation Guide says "Height of the ... Cisco ASR 9901 Router and Cisco ASR 9001 Router is 3.47 inches (8.8 cm)", which is 88.14 - and note that one sentence covers two chassis, and that 3.47 in is the ASR 9001's own data sheet figure. THE DATA SHEET IS CARRIED AND THE STENCIL IS WHY. The rear master's shape box reads 87.38 mm and its body ink, at the scale set by the body WIDTH alone, comes out 87.11 mm - a hundredth of a millimetre from the data sheet's 87.12, on an axis that was never anchored to it. The guide's sentence looks like a sibling's number reused; it is recorded here rather than dismissed.
gaps.wanted: a ruler on a real ASR 9901, or a Cisco mechanical drawing.

gaps.note: THE DISPLAY IS MODELLED AND ITS READING DIRECTION IS NOT. cisco/led-matrix-4@1 carries the guide's "one row of four characters" and the twenty-eight readings of Tables 25 and 26, so the model can be asked what this display says. THE WINDOW STANDS ON END, and that is settled. It was two drawings agreeing, which is one drawing counted twice - the stencil master and Figure 12's line art, both portrait, both hatched with diagonals, either of which could have been a draughting symbol for "display". It is not a symbol: photographs of three real units show a light rounded bezel left of the CISCO wordmark with a dark portrait window in it, and the sharpest resolves the DIAMOND LATTICE the drawings were tracing. So Cisco's "one row of four characters" reads TURNED. WHICH WAY IT TURNS IS IN NOTHING. Up or down, no document says. Fourteen resale listings for this chassis were opened and every unit photographed is POWERED OFF, so not one of them reads the matrix. The skin draws the window and nothing in it, `characters: 4` is Cisco's sentence rather than a reading of the artwork, and no rotation is claimed.
gaps.wanted: a photograph of a POWERED ASR 9901 front panel - the matrix mid-boot would read it off in one frame - or any Cisco drawing that puts characters in the window.

gaps.note: FAN 2, FAN 1 and FAN 0 are printed bottom-to-top on a narrow rail at the right of each tray, and the tray's own drawn plate covers that rail - the captive screw sits on the same strip. This model draws each tray as a filled rectangle, so the three marks land under their bays and L21 reports them. The marks are kept where the master puts them rather than moved somewhere they would render, because moving them would put ink where the device has none. It is the same defect cisco/asr-9902 and cisco/asr-9903 carry and the same fix closes all three.
gaps.wanted: cisco/asr-9901-fan@1 drawn with its flange cut away where the chassis prints the slot label, so the mark shows through.

gaps.note: The nine lamps are counted by Figure 12's callout 8 and printed by the master, and no document in the intake says what their colours mean. The guide's RP Front Panel Indicators section describes the ASR 9001's cluster and the LED matrix; Table 21, "LEDs at System Startup", covers line cards, power modules and fan trays. Searched both, plus the data sheet, for each legend by name. SO THE COLOURS ARE READ OFF THE NAMES - red for CRIT, amber for MAJ and MIN, green for SSD, GPS, SYNC and INPUT OK - and every one of the nine says so in its own description rather than leaving the reading to be inferred from the fact that a colour is written down.
gaps.wanted: a Cisco LED table for the ASR 9901 front panel.

gaps.note: THE TOP, BOTTOM AND TWO SIDES ARE SIZED AND NOT DRAWN, and each carries an `empty:` sentence saying where the search ran. No source in the intake elevates them: the stencil's 119 masters are front and rear elevations, the install guide's figures for this chassis are two elevations, a top-view FOOTPRINT (Figure 20, which dimensions the outline and draws no feature), an airflow path, a two-post mounting figure, a clearance diagram and an unpacking sequence, and the data sheet gives the envelope.
gaps.wanted: a Cisco mechanical drawing of the ASR 9901, or orthographic photographs of the top and one side with something of known size in frame.

gaps.note: cisco/asr-9901-fan@1 measures 88.62 x 81.70 mm off this chassis's rear master and cisco/asr-9902-fan@1 measures 88.58 x 82.18 off the ASR 9902's - four hundredths of a millimetre apart across and half a millimetre down, which is inside what either reading can resolve. Cisco's ordering tables give them different part numbers, ASR-9901-FAN and ASR-9902-FAN, and that is the only reason this library holds two contracts. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT is a photograph of either tray's label, or the two in one hand. If they are one part, one contract should carry both chassis and the ASR 9901's missing power figure is answered by the ASR 9902's 72 W - which is exactly why the two are not merged on a drawing's say-so.
gaps.wanted: a label photograph of an ASR-9901-FAN, or a Cisco document that dimensions either tray.

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9000 Series ASR 9902 Router - a 2 RU fixed-port aggregation services router delivering up to 800 Gbps. Two route processors across the top and the integrated fixed board below them, carrying forty-eight ports in two mirrored slices: eight SFP28, three QSFP28 and one QSFP-DD and twelve SFP+ on each. The rear carries two 1.6 kW power modules at the ends and three fan trays between them, with the power switch on the left panel and the NEBS grounding lug on the right. Airflow is front to back. Nothing seats in the front: the board is part of the chassis and there is no Port Expansion Card bay, which is what separates this from its 3 RU ASR 9903 sibling.

gaps.note: FT0, FT1 and FT2 are printed bottom-to-top on a narrow rail at the left of each tray, and the tray's own drawn plate starts on that rail rather than beside it - the captive screw sits on the same strip. This model draws each tray as a filled rectangle, so the three marks land under their bays and L21 reports them. The marks are kept where the master puts them rather than moved somewhere they would render, because moving them would put ink where the device has none. It is the same defect cisco/asr-9903's fan labels carry and the same fix closes both.
gaps.wanted: cisco/asr-9902-fan@1 drawn with its left flange cut away where the chassis prints the slot label, so the mark shows through.

gaps.note: CISCO'S OWN STENCIL AND ITS OWN DATA SHEETS DISAGREE ABOUT HOW WIDE THIS CHASSIS IS RELATIVE TO ITS SIBLING. The ASR 9902 and ASR 9903 front masters draw their bodies 1568.93 and 1569.68 art units wide, the same outline to 0.2 mm, while c78-744663 gives 439.74 mm for this chassis and c78-744035 gives 443.86 mm for the 9903. THIS FILE TAKES THE 439.74 and the evidence for that choice is a ruler inside the artwork rather than a preference: at that scale the twenty SFP-class cage columns come out on a 14.253 mm pitch against SFF-8433's 14.25, while the same measurement on the ASR 9903 at its own stated width lands on 14.36, which is 0.8 percent over a standard that does not vary. So the 9902 is the chassis the outline fits. WHAT IT COSTS IF THE READING IS WRONG is about 0.9 percent on every x on this face and on the RP slot pitch, which would go from 209.58 to 211.44.
gaps.wanted: a Cisco mechanical drawing of either chassis, or a tape measure across a real ASR 9902 and a real ASR 9903 - two numbers that would settle both models at once. Tracked in roc-ops/Portrayal#374.

gaps.note: THE TOP, BOTTOM AND TWO SIDES ARE SIZED AND NOT DRAWN, and each carries an `empty:` sentence saying where the search ran. What they have in common is that no source in the intake ELEVATES them. The Visio stencil's 119 masters are front and rear elevations and hold no plan or side view at all. The install guide's figures for this chassis are two elevations, a top-view FOOTPRINT (Figure 18, which dimensions the outline and draws no feature), an airflow path, eight rack-mounting sequences across 19-inch and 23-inch, 2-post and 4-post racks, a stacking figure and an air-filter view - the mounting figures show the sides at an angle and dimension nothing on them. The data sheet gives the envelope. WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE, from the photographs, is a cisco wordmark and a product label on the top, feet and bracket landings underneath, and a bracket rail on each side. None is positioned by anything, and drawing them by eye off a three-quarter render would put unmeasured furniture on four faces at once.
gaps.wanted: a Cisco mechanical drawing of the ASR 9902, or orthographic photographs of the top and one side with something of known size in frame.

gaps.note: The furniture strip at the right of the RP row carries a captive screw, a round dimple above it and a small dark circle between them, and the guide names none of the three. The same two unnamed features appear on the ASR 9903 in the same place. They are the right shape for an ESD wrist-strap jack and a captive-screw well, and calling them so would be a guess with a citation attached, so they are left off the face.

WHAT IS NOT SAID is whether a lamp beside a QSFP-DD running a 400G coherent module means anything different - the coherent optics section of the configuration guide describes transponder and muxponder modes and their alarms and never mentions the faceplate lamp. devices.description: Cisco ASR 9000 Series ASR 9903 Router - a 3 RU fixed-port aggregation services router delivering up to 3.6 Tbps. Everything a user touches is on the front: two route processors across the top, the integrated fixed board in the middle with sixteen 100GE QSFP28 ports and twenty 10GE SFP+ ports, and one bay below it for an optional Port Expansion Card. The rear carries four 1.6 kW power modules in a row and four fan trays below them, with the NEBS grounding lug on a fixed panel between the middle pair. Airflow is front to back.

gaps.note: TWO CISCO DOCUMENTS GIVE THIS CHASSIS TWO MAXIMUM WEIGHTS and they are not reconcilable as different scopes. Table 2 of the ASR 9903 data sheet (c78-744035) gives ASR 9903 chassis with 2 RPs, 4 PSUs and 4 FANs, 5.18 x 17.475 x 30 in. and 81.62 lb, or 131.57 x 443.86 x 762 mm and 37 kg. The fixed-port Hardware Installation Guide's Lifting Guidelines read "A fully-configured Cisco ASR 9903 can weigh as much as 70 pounds (31.75 kg)". Both are maxima and the guide's scope is the WIDER of the two - "fully configured" must include a PEC, which the data sheet's list does not - so the larger figure should have been the guide's, and it is 5.25 kg smaller. `chassis.weight-kg` carries the data sheet's 37 kg because the source table makes the data sheet authoritative for weight, and this gap carries the guide's figure so the disagreement is not silently resolved.
gaps.wanted: a scale under a real ASR 9903, or a Cisco document that states the weight with its scope spelled out.

gaps.note: The furniture strip at the right of the RP row carries four features. Two are identified and drawn: a hex grounding stud and an IEC 60417-5019 earth symbol. The other two are not. Above the stud the master draws a plain circular dimple about 3 mm across, and between them a smaller dark circle that reads as a through-hole on the install guide's Figure 3 render at 2.7 px/mm. NO SENTENCE IN THE INTAKE NAMES EITHER. They are the right shape and the right place for an ESD wrist-strap jack and a captive-screw well - the ASR 9001 has an ESD socket on its front and Figure 9 of the same guide points at it - but the ASR 9903 is not in that figure and the guide's ESD section names no socket for this chassis. Drawing them as an esd-jack would be a guess with a citation attached, so they are left off.
gaps.wanted: a callout in a Cisco figure, or a photograph of the front right corner close enough to read the two features.

gaps.note: The front master draws a recessed frame 13.51 x 26.01 mm at the left end of the fixed board with a yellow tag in it reading ATTENTION / ON-OFF, and the install guide's Figure 3 render shows the same recess with a plain white tag. WHAT IT IS, IS NOT SAID FOR THIS CHASSIS. The identical assembly on the ASR 9902's REAR is captioned in Figure 158 of the same guide with POWER printed under it and a lamp beside it, so on that chassis it is a power switch. For the ASR 9903 the guide says only that the AC and DC PSUs for ASR 9903 routers have no power switch, being plug-and-play, and that the power LED (PWR) is on the router's front, which places a PWR lamp on the front and names no switch. So the recess and its tag are drawn as panel decor and silkscreen, exactly as the artwork has them, and nothing here asserts that they are a switch.
gaps.wanted: a callout naming this feature on the ASR 9903, or a photograph of the front left corner.

gaps.note: FT0 to FT3 are printed on the chassis in a notch at the bottom left of each tray - the tray is cut away there and the label plate shows through, which is how the drawing and the guide's Figure 4 both have it. This model draws each tray as a filled rectangle, so the four marks land under their bays and L21 reports them. The marks are kept at the positions the master gives rather than moved somewhere they would render, because moving them would put ink where the device has none; the honest fix is a notched tray outline, which is a component change.
gaps.wanted: cisco/asr-9903-fan@1 drawn with its bottom-left notch, so the chassis label shows through it.

gaps.note: THE TOP, BOTTOM AND TWO SIDES ARE SIZED AND NOT DRAWN, and each carries an `empty:` sentence saying where the search ran. What they have in common is that no source in the intake ELEVATES them. The Visio stencil's 119 masters are front and rear elevations and hold no plan or side view at all. The install guide's figures for this chassis are two elevations, a top-view FOOTPRINT (Figure 19, which dimensions the outline and draws no feature), an airflow path, two rack-mounting sequences, a bracket-to-side sequence and an air-filter exploded view - the last two show the sides at an angle and dimension nothing on them. The data sheet gives the envelope. WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE, from the photographs, is a cisco wordmark and a large product label on the top, four feet and the bracket landings underneath, and a bracket rail on each side. None is positioned by anything, and drawing them by eye off a three-quarter render would put unmeasured furniture on four faces at once.
gaps.wanted: a Cisco mechanical drawing of the ASR 9903, or orthographic photographs of the top and one side with something of known size in frame.

gaps.note: NEITHER THE FAN TRAY NOR THE ROUTE PROCESSOR CARRIES A DRAW FIGURE MEASURED ON THIS CHASSIS, and the L27 and L29 warnings are left standing as the record. The one per-FRU table in the intake is a `show environment` example in the fixed-port guide's troubleshooting chapter, and it was taken on an ASR 9902: its rows read ASR-9902-LC 614/283, A99-RP-F 102/43 and ASR-9902-FAN 72/7. Cards mount VERTICALLY and the redundant RSP pair takes the OUTER slots, 0 and 5, with four line cards between them. Modelled as a BARE CAGE; the card openings are cutouts rather than bays - see gaps.

Table 14's "Power Dissipation" row says only "Use the Cisco Power Calculator ... to estimate the maximum power distribution", so the chassis total is whatever its occupants sum to. gaps.note: THESE BAY DIMENSIONS ARE A MODELLING STANDARD AND NOT MEASUREMENTS OF THIS CAGE. Every slot bay is 41.4 x 395.7 with a 41.4 x 355.6 opening, the envelope now shared by every full-size ASR 9000 card (see asr9000-card-standard). Earlier revisions grew these bays to 42.67 x 403.40 to satisfy a fit check against one accepted card, which a fit check would pass just as readily if both sides were wrong; that is gone, but a standard is not a measurement either. What each figure rests on: 395.7 is the Cisco "includes ejector bracket/lever" envelope and agrees with a lab measurement of a real RSP-880; 355.6 is the Table A-10 plate length; 41.4 is the thickness Cisco states most often and has not been measured. What IS independently grounded here is the cage, measured off the stencil at 260.52 x 364.32 and corroborated by the printed slot labels, and the 43.42 pitch. The measured cage height is 8.72 mm taller than the 355.6 opening now drawn, a difference the standard accepts rather than explains.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned figure giving the clear opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, or a caliper reading of a card thickness, either of which would replace a standard figure with a measured one

gaps.note: The vertical power shelf is drawn as one opening rather than three module openings. Figure 21 and Table 15 both establish three modules stacked M0 at the bottom to M2 at the top, so the count and numbering are not in doubt; the boundaries are. The master draws this column POPULATED - each module rendered with its own fan wheel - so a scan returns grille detail rather than separators, the same obstacle the ASR 9904's horizontal shelf presents. The column's outer rectangle is measured and drawn.

gaps.note: The ASR 9906's rear carries the fabric card cage and we know a great deal ABOUT it and almost nothing about its geometry. There is no ASR-9906 Rear master in Cisco's stencil, and Figure 21 shows only the front. The count is sourced but indirectly: Table 13 quotes the configured weight for a chassis "Configured with two fan trays, two RSPs, five fabric cards, and one PEM", so five, and the sibling ASR 9910's Figure 22 shows fabric slots numbered from 0. Nothing states their width, their height, or where the PEM sits. The rear is therefore sized and carries regions naming what is there. ONE CUTOUT NOW EXISTS ON THIS FACE and it is not an exception to that: the NEBS grounding receptacle, which Table 12 states and Figure 61 shows, on an offset borrowed from the sibling chassis rather than measured - see provenance/grounding. The fabric card cage is still not drawn and is no better sourced than it was.
gaps.wanted: an ASR 9906 rear elevation, or a rear photograph

gaps.note: THE BOTTOM IS THE ONLY FACE OF THIS CHASSIS WITH NO SOURCE, and it is not a gap in this file's research. gaps.note: THESE BAY DIMENSIONS WERE GROWN TO MEET A COMPONENT AND ARE NOT MEASUREMENTS. Each was set by taking the size of a card the bay accepts, because a fit check reported the bay as too small. On this chassis: 492.10 on 5 bays - a99-sfc3-s, 492.10 long The ten card bays left this list when they took the family standard, 41.4 x 395.7 (see asr9000-card-standard). The danger is specific and it is why they are listed rather than left to look like geometry. A fit check compares a bay to a component and NEITHER of them to the world, so it is satisfied by both being wrong together exactly as easily as by both being right. Every mismatch resolved by moving one side removes the signal without adding any truth, and once resolved nothing will flag it again. These are the entries where that happened, so the record survives the check going quiet. What IS independently grounded and is not in this list: the cage extents, measured off the stencil and confirmed on several chassis by printed slot labels or a card guide rail; the slot pitch; the 395.70 fourth-generation envelope, which is Cisco's own "includes ejector bracket/lever" figure; and the shapesheet sizes for the power modules and fan trays. gaps.note: The guide states that line cards are installed upside down in slots 10 through 19 of the bottom card cage but right side up in slots 0 through 9 of the top card cage. This is a real property of the chassis and the model cannot currently express it. The bays for 10 to 19 are geometrically identical to 0 to 9 and carry no rotation, because the card is inverted about its own long axis rather than rotated in the plane of the panel - a `rotate: 180` would spin the faceplate end for end, which is a different thing and would put the ejectors at the wrong ends. So a card rendered in slot 15 will show its ports and its part number the same way up as one in slot 5, and on real hardware it would not. Anyone reading port positions off the lower cage should know that.

gaps.note: THE REAL MACHINE HAS THREE LEVELS AND THIS MODEL HAS TWO. Overview and Reference Guide, "Cisco ASR 9922 Router Power Modules": "ASR-9922 supports: Four AC PEMs (power shelves). Version 2 supports four power supplies and version 3 supports three power supplies", and for DC "Four DC PEMs. Each PEM supports up to four power supplies." So the chassis holds four shelves and each shelf holds the supplies; this face draws sixteen supply bays directly, which is 4 x 4 flattened. WHAT THAT COSTS IS FOUR SOURCED PARTS WITH NOWHERE TO GO. cisco/a9k-power-tray is the version 2 shelf, cisco/a9k-ac-pem-v3 and cisco/a9k-dc-pem-v3 are the version 3 shelves - all three drawn off stencil masters at 468.12 x 48.03 - and cisco/a9k-power-shelf-cover is the blank for one. They are unplaced because there is no shelf bay to seat them in, not because nobody knows where they belong: the guide names them by PID against this chassis. THE SIXTEEN BAYS ARE NOT WRONG, and this is why the flattening has stood: a version 2 shelf holds four supplies and 4 x 4 is sixteen, so the supply positions are right for the V2 build. They are wrong for V3, which puts three supplies in a shelf - twelve, not sixteen - and that difference is invisible while the shelves are not there. See roc-ops/Portrayal#262.

devices.description: The CH3000 headend optics platform - a 3RU, 19-inch mid-plane chassis for cable headend and hub optics, designed by Aurora Networks (2004), sold under the ARRIS name and now by CommScope / Vistance. Sixteen identical full-depth slots take transmitters, receivers, amplifiers and a power supply from the front; the rear of each slot takes the module's dynamic back plate, which carries its optical and RF connections, or a half-depth passive. A mid-plane between the two carries the 12 VDC bus and the RS-485 management bus.

gaps.note: a front blank is named once: the FA3500 data sheet's ordering note ships "a BP3000 blank face plate" with the FA3524S, for the front of the slot its double-wide back plate leaves empty. No document draws or photographs a BP3000, and no rear blank is named in any of the 164 data sheets held; a rear plate legended BP3001 appears beside a BP-P2 in the CX3003C sheet's photograph and is probably the rear blank, but no document names or describes it.
gaps.wanted: a photograph or drawing of the BP3000 front blank, and the part number of the rear blank

gaps.note: the PS3006D and PS3006N on the HT3580H chassis photograph carry an older face - a 3.5 mm jack legended Serial in place of the micro-USB, and vertical vent slots on the PS3006N - than the PS3006 data sheet's own photographs. The current face is modelled.
gaps.wanted: the revision history of the PS3006 faceplate

gaps.note: the HT3580H data sheet names three back plates for a CA3008 carrier and photographs one, the BD31A8-100-H10F modelled here. The BD31A8-100-H18F (eight BC inputs, no NC) and the BD35M8 mux plates (-ACx and -EEx with three SC/APC, -DCx with six LC/APC, each with nine F-type inputs) are described in text only, so their layouts are not drawn.
gaps.wanted: a face-on photograph or drawing of a BD31A8-100-H18F and of a BD35M8

gaps.note: the FA3524S ships with a double-wide BP-F3 back plate (three SC/APC ports for its input and two outputs) that leaves the neighbouring slot empty for cooling, per the FA3500 data sheet's ordering note 2. The BP-F2, BP-F2-AL and BP-F4 are drawn in that sheet; the BP-F3 is not, so an FA3524S can be seated but its back plate is not modelled.
gaps.wanted: a drawing or photograph of the BP-F3

gaps.note: the chassis data sheets state the arrangement - "32 half-depth slots (16 front-loaded and 16 rear-loaded)" and "32 midplane electrical interconnects (16 front and 16 rear)", and the OR3144H sheet says a half-depth module can be plugged in from either side - so a half-depth module seats in a slot's front bay or in its rear bay, where a full-depth module's back plate would go, and that is how the half-depth modules modelled here seat. No photograph held shows one installed, front or rear, to confirm its face against the slot. Not modelled: the DT3550N transmitter, whose data sheet has no face image; the 8- and 10-channel CWDM demultiplexers (NP34D08, NP34D10, OP34D8C, OP34D10C), whose data-sheet photographs are the multiplexer's artwork relabelled - they print "CWDM MUX" where the photographed 5-channel demux prints "CWDM DEMUX", and the OP34D10C sheet's image is labelled OP34M10C; the OP3168P and OP3178P octal PON filters, whose faces are a dense grid of LC adapters with legends the data-sheet photographs do not resolve; the NP31F08S06 RFoG filter, which has no face image; and the 8x8 splitters (NP38S08, OP38S8S), which are two slots wide and only drawn.
gaps.wanted: a photograph of a CH3000 with half-depth modules seated, front and rear

gaps.note: several half-depth families are modelled as the one variant their data sheet photographs, and the others would present a different port set: OP33F1x as the single OP33F1S (the dual OP33F1D has six ports); NP35C0x as the NP35C01D03 red/blue split (the family also takes CWDM/DWDM and DWDM-group splits, single or dual, with an optional test port, each legended differently); and OP35F4S as the variant with a -20 dB test port (the test port is optional). Each would need its own photograph.
gaps.wanted: face photographs of the OP33F1D, the other NP35C0x variants and an OP35F4S without a test port

an `attrs.performance` section; one of `power-max-w`, `power-max-ac-w`, `power-max-dc-w` in `attrs.power`; one of `operating-temp`, `operating-temp-f2b`, `operating-temp-b2f` in `attrs.environmental` (profile `optical` - see spec/schemas/profiles.yaml) - unlocks the About panel, and comparison against other devices

datasheet.title: Dell PowerEdge R660 Spec Sheet

devices.description: 1U two-socket rack server, 16th generation - up to ten 2.5 inch front drive bays (or eight with a Smart Flow vent, sixteen EDSFF E3.S, or none), two 60 mm power supplies at opposite ends of the rear, up to three PCIe slots, an OCP NIC 3.0 slot and a rear BOSS-N1 boot module

gaps.note: TG table 14 lists riser configuration 0 (no riser) and 9 (R2S + R3S, two rear EDSFF E3.S drives with low-profile slots 1 and 3), and ISM figure 13 shows configuration 9's rear at a resolution that confirms the layout but cannot be measured; the VisioCafe set draws neither.
gaps.wanted: a straight-on rear photograph or a vector master of either configuration

gaps.note: Dell's service model carries risers 2A and 3A and no other, so the top view draws risers 2 and 3 for every variant sharing their cages and leaves riser 2Q (configuration 6) and the full-height risers 1P and 4P (configuration 3) out, rather than borrow an outline. The model also begins both risers 20 mm behind the rear wall; the plans are clipped at the wall.
gaps.wanted: a service model, figure or top photograph with riser 2Q or the full-height risers fitted

gaps.note: the ISM makes the LOM card optional and offers a Management Interface Card (MIC, with Dell DPU cards only) in its place, and a different rear I/O board with the liquid-cooling (DLC) module. Every rear master held draws the LOM card and the standard board, and figures 220-222 show the others only in isometric, so the lom bay accepts only the LOM card and the rio bay only the standard board; what fills the LOM window when neither card is fitted is not known.
gaps.wanted: a straight-on rear image of an R660 without a LOM card, with a MIC, or with the liquid-cooling rear I/O board

gaps.note: the ISM requires an EDSFF E3.S drive blank in every empty E3.S slot ("Removing an EDSFF E3.S drive blank", figures 77/78, isometric) and no straight-on image of one is held. The E3.S bays default to dell/e3s-carrier-blank@1, the carrier's own face without its lamps, legend and label - the way Dell's 2.5 inch blank is its carrier - so the fronts do not draw empty; that face is an estimate. Whether an empty COLUMN takes four blanks or one dell/e3s-filler-1u@1 is also unsettled.
gaps.wanted: a straight-on photograph of a single-slot E3.S blank, or of an R660 E3.S front with empty slots

gaps.note: ISM figure 4 draws the 16 x E3.S build's left ear as a plain strip without the status glyphs the 14-drive figure shows, and neither figure prints bay numbers; the E3.S fronts here seat the same left panel as every other front and number down each column like the 2.5 inch bays.
gaps.wanted: a straight-on photograph of a 16 x E3.S R660 front

datasheet.title: Dell EMC PowerEdge R740xd Spec Sheet

devices.description: 2U two-socket rack server - 24 x 2.5 inch front drive bays

gaps.note: dell/riser-divider-plate-14g@1's OUTLINE AND DEPTH ARE MEASURED and its FACE IS NOT. Both bodies come off Dell's service model to the hundredth - face 267.32..278.64 and 297.10..308.42, y 1.81..42.42, 17.61 proud - but what is printed or punched on them has not been established from any figure. Riser 1's equivalent plate carries a five-slot column that appears in no cut of the model at any plane and had to be read off ISM figure 8; whether these two carry the same column, or anything else, was NOT SEARCHED FOR rather than looked for and found absent. The recess drawn for the card clip is drawn because a clip sits in a recess on riser 1, not because this plate was seen to have one.
gaps.wanted: a rear photograph or ISM figure at usable resolution across face 267..309, which would settle both plates at once - they are the same pressing

gaps.note: WHICH OF THE TWO IS IN FRONT IS ASSERTED, NOT MEASURED. dell/riser-1-top- shelf-14g@1 is 14.68 proud (measured, the chassis shell's front) and dell/riser-1-shroud-14g@1's plate is extruded at 17.76 (an approximation across a whole outline, as that file's depth key says), so the plate drew in front and the shelf read as tucked under the piece it closes the top of. The operator, looking at the render against the hardware, says the shelf is the outermost thing there. It is expressed as a 3.10 `lift` on the composition - the smallest value that clears 17.76 - so both measured depths survive untouched and only the ordering changes. If the plate's width and depth are ever settled properly (see riser-1-shroud-rib-width-unresolved, which is the same piece of missing evidence) this lift should be re-derived rather than kept.
gaps.wanted: a mechanical drawing or a caliper on the hardware giving the riser-1 shroud plate's front and the chassis top shelf's front at the same face x, which is the one measurement that settles the ordering outright

gaps.note: THE MID BAYS ARE NOT NUMBERED HERE, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. This device numbers its front drives 0 to 23 and its rear drives 12 to 15 or 24 to 27, in both cases because Dell's own label says so and the numbering was checked against it. NOTHING FOUND SO FAR SAYS WHAT DELL CALLS THE FOUR MID-BAY DRIVES. They are `mid-lff-0..3` and `mid-sff-0..3`, which are positions and not claims: they say "the four slots, left to right" and assert nothing about what the machine prints or what iDRAC reports. Inventing a range that looked like the others - 24 to 27 say - would have been the easy thing and would have been a fabrication of exactly the kind the front and rear numbering was careful to avoid.
gaps.wanted: the mid-drive-tray page of the R740xd installation and service manual, or a photograph of the tray with its silkscreen legible

gaps.note: THE PREVIOUS FORM OF THIS GAP SAID THE CAD POSE WAS EXPLODED. IT IS NOT, AND THE SENTENCE IS KEPT HERE BECAUSE IT IS THE INSTRUCTIVE PART. A reading of R740XD_GPU_Brackets_01-1 was rejected on the grounds that its y extent ran -40 to +24 against an 86.8 mm panel - "not a seated pose". That was a Y-CONVENTION ARTEFACT IN THE READER, not a fact about the model. Calibrated against the rear handle, whose device y is trusted, the convention is face_y = 86.8 - raw_y; it reproduces the handle's low edge at 42.35 to the hundredth and this assembly's own sibling R740XD_Expansioncard_Clip-1.001 at y 1.81..44.81, the figure riser-1-shroud-14g already carried from an independent read. The pose is seated and the 36.9 mm was real all along - a plausibility check that fires on the reader instead of the data rejects good evidence, and it cost a wrong fix at the other end of the part. WHAT THE MODEL ACTUALLY SHOWS, descended to mesh children, is two levels: Body_2_3.002 at 111.70..148.60, 11.06 proud - a wide lower shelf, now drawn - and Body_1_3.005 at 125.00..135.10, 17.71 proud - a narrow rib. WHAT IS STILL OPEN is the rib. riser-1-shroud-14g draws it 120.64..137.26, about 4 mm wider on each side than the body at that depth. The outline came from cad-outline.py cutting at the panel plane, which returns the SILHOUETTE of everything the plane crosses rather than one body, so it cannot settle a single body's width. Re-cutting it would move the slot column and the clip recess, both photo-measured off ISM figure 8 and both currently agreeing with the render, so it is recorded rather than guessed. RE-READ WHEN THE STRIP UNDER RISER 1 WAS RETIRED, and still open. The same model was cut across face y 66.24..68.05 under the riser, and nothing there stands in front of the rear sheet (Body_8_6, z 708.88 at most, behind fillers whose fronts reach 718.03). That settles the band below the plate and says nothing new about the rib above it.
gaps.wanted: a mechanical drawing of the riser-1 shroud, or a clean section of R740XD_GPU_Brackets_01-1 above the shelf, to settle the raised rib's width independently of the panel-plane silhouette

gaps.note: THE NUMBER CAME FROM A DESCRIPTION, NOT A MEASUREMENT. std/vga@1 stands 6.73 proud because that is what a D-sub does when its flange bolts through sheet metal, and on this machine's front the connector is on the control panel board, which sits back from the bezel - so only a little of it emerges. The operator, looking at the hardware, put that at "a millimetre and a half"; `inset: 5.23` is 6.73 less 1.50 and is therefore an estimate dressed as two decimal places. IT IS THE SETBACK THAT IS UNKNOWN, not the connector. The 6.73 is TE 114-40010's mating dimension and stays; what nobody here has measured is how far behind the faceplate the board sits. A caliper on the hardware, or any drawing that dimensions the control panel board against the front bezel, replaces one number and nothing else. THE REAR D-SUBS ARE NOT AFFECTED. They bolt through the rear panel in the ordinary way and carry no inset.
gaps.wanted: the control panel board's setback from the front bezel, measured

gaps.note: TWO NUMBERS, ONE APPEARANCE EACH, AND NEITHER CORROBORATED. This device seats both supplies at y 46.20, and the only other place that number appears is a comment on riser 2's plate saying the plate was cut back to "face 46.20 - the power supply's top edge", which cites this seating rather than a source. psu-1100w-ac-14g's provenance used to argue the module top was y 45.0, read off R740 ISM figure 9 - but it argued that in the same breath as a height of 41.8, and the height has since been measured off Dell's own service model at 39.1. A position argued from a reading whose companion number is disproven is not evidence for the position. THE CAD CANNOT ANSWER IT. glb-parts.py states the rule it enforces: sizes survive a pose and positions do not, and this scene draws the supply with its withdrawal handle swung open for a removal procedure. The body measures cleanly at 86.3 x 39.1 x 195.5 and its face y lands nowhere near either candidate. AN ATTEMPT TO RE-READ FIGURE 9 FAILED GATE 1 AT 13.18%, against a provenance that claims 0.26% for the same figure - so the failure is in the panel detection, not in the figure, and nothing may be taken off it until somebody finds the body's true top and bottom edges in that raster. The seating is left where it is rather than moved on a measurement that did not pass its own gate. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the body edges in ISM figure 9 identified by hand rather than by ink-density, which turns the 13.18% back into the 0.26% the figure is capable of and makes the fraction readable. 1.2 mm is worth one careful pass, because riser 2's plate is cut to this number.
gaps.wanted: the supply's top edge on the rear face, from a figure that has passed Gate 1

gaps.note: Dell's model carries riser 1 (three-slot, measured here to the tenth) and the low-profile riser 2C. It carries no full-height riser 2 and no riser 3. Their bodies - the PCB and the slot connectors in `body.boxes` on dell/riser-2a/2d/2e/2f-14g and dell/riser-3a/3b-14g - are riser 1's, stood at their own bays' outer edges, and riser 3's PCB is cut to end at the supply cage it stands on.
gaps.wanted: A model or a photograph of riser 2A and riser 3 seated, which would put both PCBs where they are.

gaps.note: ISM figures 17 and 18 number five fronts - 24, 16 and 8 x 2.5 inch at bays 0-23, 0-15 and 0-7, and 12 and 8 x 3.5 inch at 0-11 and 0-7. TWO OF THE FIVE ARE NOW DRAWN. `front` is the 24 x 2.5 inch; `front-lff-12` is the 12 x 3.5 inch, the one that mattered, because it is the front the rears numbered 12-15 and 12-13 belong to. It is a variant view with `face: front`, bound by the `lff12-` configurations, and its grid was measured off dellr740xd-12x35.webp at Gate 1 0.07% - the same backplane opening the 24 SFF bays divide, 428.832 / 4 = 107.208 against a measured period of 107.216. THE 16 AND 8 x 2.5 INCH AND THE 8 x 3.5 INCH ARE STILL NOT MODELLED, and no figure for them has been measured.
gaps.wanted: the remaining three fronts as further `face: front` variants, each with a configuration to bind it.

gaps.note: DELL ENUMERATES THEM. ISM table 28, "Supported backplane options for PowerEdge R740XD systems", lists front, mid and rear together - ten rows, and the coupling falls straight out: 2.5in x24 no rear 2.5in x24 + 2.5in x4 mid + 2.5in x4 rear 2.5in x24 (20 SAS/SATA + 4 NVMe) no rear 3.5in x12 no rear 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x4 mid + 3.5in x2 rear 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x4 mid + 2.5in x4 rear 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x2 rear 3.5in x12 + 2.5in x4 rear 2.5in x24 NVMe no rear 3.5in x12 Hybrid with NVMe U.2 no rear The 24-bay front takes ONE rear, the 4 x 2.5 inch, which figure 19 numbers 24-27. The 12-bay front takes either, and figure 19 numbers both from 12. This device carries the 24-bay front, which is why its rear reads 24-27. THE ARITHMETIC GOT THERE FIRST AND IS NOW REDUNDANT. Bays numbered 12-15 imply eleven bays this model does not have; that is how the error was found. Table 28 is how it is now SOURCED, and a guess agreeing with a document afterwards is worth more than either alone. THE RISER SIDE IS TABLE 25, and its discriminator is riser 2 rather than riser 3. Rear storage is offered in riser configurations 0, 1 and 2 and no others: 1 and 2 fit a one-slot low-profile riser 2 (2B or 2C, slot 4 only), while configuration 3 fits a three-slot 2A (slots 4, 5, 6) and has NO rear storage despite fitting no riser 3 at all. It is riser 2's full-height section that occupies the bay the rear cage needs. This device's configurations already encode exactly that - rear storage only with rc0, rc1 and rc2 - and row 3 is `rc3-1a2a`, added when the riser 3 opening and rear storage bay 3 turned out to be the SAME HOLE, closed by two different blanks depending on which configuration you picked. RE-READ AND STILL OPEN: that change touched which bay closes an opening, not the front-to-rear coupling this gap is about. Re-read again when riser 1's brackets moved 1 mm and slot 2 lost its numeral on 1A - both are ink and geometry inside one bay, and neither reaches across faces. Re-read a third time when riser 1's plate grew to meet the slot strip and the shroud: the bay's own box moved, and still nothing crossed a face. A fourth time when riser 2's three slots were aligned and its plate cut back to the full-height pair. That one surfaced a NEW question but not a new gap of this kind: a bay's occupant is drawn after the panel, so a card cannot be shown "only through its cutout" without a part drawn after the bays to mask it. Recorded where it belongs, on the riser 2 slot 6 cutout, rather than widened into this one. A fifth time when the screw tab was split out of the frame so it could draw in front of riser 2's bracket tails. That is a draw-order fact about one bay, not a coupling between faces. A sixth time when riser 3 became bay 1 reflected - mirrored brackets, a two-slot plate and its own slot strip. Handedness is a fact about one bay's own metal and reaches no further than that. A seventh time when riser 3 slid 9.525 right to sit over the power supply's edge. Moving one bay along its own face changes nothing about which front it can be sold with. An eighth time when two "rivet" pairs beside the divider turned out to be card retention clips. A misread of what is on the rear, corrected on the rear, and silent about any front. A ninth time when those rivets came back, scoped: they are what the riser cage mounts to and they show when drives are fitted instead. That one is a rear configuration telling two rear drawings apart, which is the mechanism this gap says is MISSING between faces - and still is. A tenth time when the C20 supply became its own part. A second occupant for an existing bay, on the same face, coupled to nothing at the front. TWO SOURCES DISAGREE AND ARE LEFT DISAGREEING. The system information label draws FIVE fronts - 24, 16 and 8 x 2.5 inch, 12 and 8 x 3.5 inch - where table 28 lists TWO front backplanes. Whether the 16- and 8-bay fronts are different chassis or one backplane drawn part-populated, nothing held here says. AND TABLE 28 HAS A MID DRIVE TRAY in three of its ten rows. This device models no mid bay at all, which is a whole third drive location missing rather than a detail.
gaps.wanted: NOW DEMONSTRABLE RATHER THAN HYPOTHETICAL. `rear-2-lff` draws a correct 2 x 3.5 inch rear on a 24 x 2.5 inch front, and ISM table 28 lists no such machine - every row carrying that rear has a 12-bay front. The mismatch even forced an id: the figure prints 12 and 13, which are already two of this chassis's front bays, so the rear ones had to be rear-drive-12 and rear-drive-13. An id clash is what this gap looks like from the inside. RE-READ AFTER THE REAR BAYS WERE SEPARATED, and still open. The rear half of this is now expressible: the chassis structure across bays 2 and 3 is its own always-present part, and what each bay holds - drives, PCIe, a blank - varies independently of the other. That was the piece `only-in` could not reach while one 287 mm component owned both bays. WHAT REMAINS IS THE FRONT. The 24 x 2.5 inch and 12 x 3.5 inch fronts are different panels, not different occupancy, and until the second is drawn nothing exercises the face-binding that would couple it to a rear. A way for a configuration to constrain more than one view at once. Today `only-in` scopes a bay to a configuration and every view chooses independently, so nothing stops a consumer selecting a 24-bay front and a rear numbered 12-15 - a machine that cannot be bought. The library needs either configurations that span views, or a declared incompatibility between them; and this device needs its 12 x 3.5 inch front modelled before either can be exercised, which is the same gap `rear-2-lff` already stands on.
